newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Most EMU aspirants seen missing targets.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Most EMU aspirants seen missing targets.

text.p: Fourteen of 15 EU members are likely to miss targets set for joining Europe's single currency, but they may not be denied entry if they make efforts to meet them, economists polled by Reuters said in a survey published on Monday.

Ratings by 34 banks and institutions across Europe of the various state's ability to meet the demands of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) showed that if criteria were strictly applied, 12 countries would have too heavy debt-to-GDP ratios. Nine would fail under the weight of budget deficits.
Even Germany would stumble on both these entry hurdles.
A related Reuters poll of a separate group of 41 European economists and political analysts predicted an 82 percent chance of EMU being launched on time on January 1, 1999.
The first wave EMU club was most likely to comprise Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

"It won't so much be the paragons in the first wave, but countries with a track record," said Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International in London. "Countries like Spain and Italy haven't been doing it long enough."
Joining EMU at the start would depend on politicians' willingness to interpret the criteria favourably in cases of marginal misses.

"If you're France and you come in at 3.4 (deficit as a percentage of GDP) then you might be in, but if you're Spain and come in at 3.4 you might not be," said Steven Englander, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris. "You get points for having been a hard currency for 10 years."
European monetary union targets envisage that each member posts a public sector deficit at three percent or less of gross domestic product in 1997.
A clear majority in the survey put France at between 3 and 3.5 percent. On Spain, 10 out of 25 put it at 3.0-3.5 percent and nine placed it on the next rung between 3.5 and 4.5 percent.

"France gets looked at differently, or even the UK, because they've gone to the wall to preserve their exchange rates, Smith Barney's Englander said. The other countries are going to yell bloody murder of course."

"It seems that creative accounting is clearly allowed by the (European) Commission and I don't see why they should allow it for France and Italy and not for Ireland," said Carlo Favero, professor of economics at Bocconi University in Milan.

Favero said Ireland -- marked as a close front-runner by 88 percent of respondents to the Reuters poll on which countries would be first -- could squeeze its fiscal deficit by just one percent of GDP to fit. The poll showed that Ireland scored badly on debt-to-GDP but economists said it, along with Denmark, had effectively been "pardoned" from having to meet this criterion.

Most countries scored well on the criteria governing inflation and long-term government bond yields. On the Exchange Rate Mechanism, which currently excludes four countries, the poll predicted Italy would be in by the end of this year.
There was no question among economists that Britain, which left the currency grid in 1992 and is wavering over whether to join EMU, would not put sterling back in ERM by the end of this year.

Of those tipped to be in the first wave, Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands scored poorly on debt, predicted to have a debt-to-GDP ratio of 70 percent or more, compared with the EMU reference level of 60 percent.
France would miss only the deficit criterion and Germany would slip into the bracket below the target level for both debt and deficit, but would still qualify.
The one that really matters is the deficit, but being more than one bracket away would be a real disqualifier, said Gibbs at Nomura.

"Almost all the countries...will make determined efforts using whatever means such as spending freezes to get to exactly three percent or less...I'm not calling it a fudge -- a number of things are quite legitimate -- but they are more or less cosmetic," she said.

Countries like Italy and France, which have faced strong public opposition to government plans to hoist taxes and cut spending, would have trouble maintaining EMU discipline in 1998 and beyond, she noted.
Some economists saw some countries, such as Italy, entering around two years later than the first wave if they continued to show efforts to converge.
"Some compromise will be battered out, because it's of such concern to the leaders that (EMU) be stable initially. And they clearly don't believe it will be," said Gibbs.
